Q: Is idempotency really necessary for preventing duplicate payments in a typical shopping mall application? A:

Yes — but not for the reason the question assumes.

Idempotency isn't a defence against the user clicking twice. It's a property that makes the same logical operation safe to apply more than once, no matter which path delivers it. Your front end guards exactly one of those paths: the one you can see. In every production duplicate I've had to unpick, there was no second click at all.

Concrete ones, all of which happened in systems that already had a disabled button and a redirect:

The provider delivers the same webhook more than once, by design. PSPs retry until they get a 2xx. If your handler needs 35 seconds and their read timeout is 30, they have already queued a retry while your first call is still committing. You apply the same transition twice. The browser isn't involved.

Your own timeout job races a late callback. You schedule a one-shot "cancel this order if it's still unpaid in N minutes". The customer pays at N plus a few seconds. The job cancels the order, the success callback lands right after it. Now you've taken money against a cancelled order — or applied both transitions — depending on which handler wins.

A transient error gets rewrapped, so the retry never happens, and then a human "fixes" it. A worker fails to take a row lock; an intermediate layer catches that transient error and re-raises it as a domain validation error. The retry policy matches on exception type, so a race that was designed to be retried becomes a permanent failure on the first attempt. The payment sits half-processed. Someone in the back office then nudges the status by hand to force a callback resend — and every manual transition emits another event and, in a system where transitions move money, actually moves it. The duplicate was created by the repair, not by the customer.

"We returned 200" is not "we applied it". A receiver can answer 200 and do nothing: the entity was already in a terminal state, or the signature didn't verify and the endpoint returns 200 deliberately so the sender stops retrying. The sender's delivery log is green, the receiver's state is wrong, and both sides are telling the truth. Until the response body says what was actually applied, you can't tell delivered-and-applied from delivered-and-dropped — and when you finally notice, the usual repair is a manual replay, which is the previous bullet.

The reconciliation job re-applies what the callback just fixed. Whatever sweeps up stuck payments will eventually pick one up in the gap between the callback committing and the new status being visible to it.

(The load-balancer retry another answer mentions is the same family — the request arriving more than once without the user doing anything.)

What actually helps, roughly in order of payoff:

  • Put the key on the operation, server side, and persist it before you call the PSP. That's the answer to your follow-up in the comments: a client-generated key only covers the client's own retry. A record written before the charge is what lets you recover the case that costs real money — you charged successfully and crashed before writing the result.
  • Make the state machine refuse illegal transitions loudly instead of trusting the caller. A terminal status should be terminal, and trying to leave it should raise rather than silently pass or silently no-op.
  • Be careful deduplicating on the provider's event id. Some providers reuse one id across all the status changes of a payment rather than issuing one per delivery attempt. Dedup on it and you'll silently drop legitimate transitions.
  • Log what you applied, not just what you received, and say so in the response body, so the sender can tell the difference.
  • Never let a single scheduled task be the only path into a terminal state. Put a periodic sweep behind it that reconciles against the provider's API instead of waiting for a callback.

None of these are prevented by front-end controls, because in none of them is there a second user action. That's the population of duplicates idempotency exists for.

Q: How to ignore "unused expression" warning from Pylance when using bit-shift operator to compose relationships in airflow A:

You can avoid unused expression warnings by using chain() instead of the bit-shift operators.

from airflow.sdk import chain

# Replaces task1 >> task2 >> task3 >> task4
chain(task1, task2, task3, task4)

# Replaces task1 >> task2 >> [task3, task4]
chain(task1, task2, [task3, task4]

Source: Airflow documentation: Dags - Task Dependencies

Q: Django ORM Q and Async A:

Q objects work in async queries the same as in sync. Q only builds the expression, it never hits the DB, so there's no async variant to look for. Only the query execution is async.

With django-async-backend, which runs queries on a real async connection (psycopg async), Q goes through filter/exclude/complex_filter as usual:

from django.db.models import Q

async for book in Book.async_object.filter(Q(name="foo") | Q(name="bar")):
    print(book.id)

count = await Book.async_object.filter(Q(name="foo")).acount()

Q: Set Quarto chunk options such as fig-height from an R object or expression A:

Use !expr in Quarto chunk options to provide values from your environment as options. This way you can calculate the height based on your data, and pass the value to the fig-height option. You need to render the Quarto document to see the resulting height.

Here is a reproducible example:

---
title: "Plot height test"
format: 
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---

With parametrized Quarto reports, certain figures are expected to grow or shrink in widht/height based on existing data. This Quarto report demonstrates how to automatically adjust figure height based on the number of rows present in data. A horizontal column plot (where Y values are groups and X values are a continuous variable, so that bars grow sideways) of fixed height would simply shrink all columns to make them fit in the default height, but in this example, the plot height itself will increase according to the number of rows, so that all plots will have roughly the same column widths.

```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)

rows <- 23
```

Data will have `{r} rows` rows.

```{r data}
data <- data.frame(
  group = letters[1:rows],
  values = sample(10:90, rows, replace = TRUE)
)
```

```{r height}
base <- 0.3
height <- base * nrow(data)
```

Based on `{r} nrow(data)` rows, with a base height of `{r} base` per row, plot height will be `{r} height`.

```{r plot}
#| fig-height: !expr height
#| fig-width: 5
data |> 
  ggplot() +
  aes(values, group) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_classic()
```
